input.reason: The preregistered prediction (accuracy 0.70–1.00 on fresh unassisted transfer) was met: 3/3 unseen, unassisted, independent-probe items correct at 100%, so the transfer claim is supported at the Quest evidence limit. But the theory's specific misconception clause was not upheld — it predicted stalling and repetition when a second arrangement was demanded, and the Shape-Shifting Crate produced a re-grouping of 24 as 6 groups of 4 alongside a constrained missing-factor solve with no stall and no frustration in 75s. The uniqueness misconception therefore looks resolved on the transfer items, though the original baseline error ("only one pair") was never directly re-tested with an impossibility judgment: Lab Learner has never been observed declaring an arrangement impossible, only producing ones that work. So the hypothesis is revised rather than supported outright. Boss eligibility is satisfied on fresh, correct, unassisted Quest evidence, so the next instrument is unseen synthesis: hold several constraints at once, decide which products can satisfy them and which cannot, and defend the impossible case. Boss ends awaiting calibration; it cannot certify mastery.
preserve: Physical rearrangement of a fixed quantity — the child moves objects, and the count stays constant while the shape changes
Short dense runtime near 75 seconds per decision phase with no filler between challenges
Constraint-driven missing factor: a rule is stated, the child must find the number that satisfies it
Immediate visible verification — the arrangement itself shows whether it worked, before any words appear
change: Multiple constraints must hold simultaneously instead of one at a time
Some demands are impossible, and declaring impossibility is a required winning move, not a giving-up move
The child must choose which quantity to work with, not just how to arrange a given one
Real loss: wrong commitments destroy stock that cannot be recovered
testNext: Whether Lab Learner can hold two constraints at once (row count AND row length bounds) rather than satisfying one and ignoring the other
Whether Lab Learner will assert 'impossible' for a prime or badly-constrained quantity instead of forcing a near-miss arrangement
Whether the factor-pair uniqueness misconception is fully gone when the product is not pre-chosen for them
Whether accuracy holds when a wrong move has a visible permanent cost
nextEvidenceRequired: At least one unseen item where the correct response is a justified impossibility claim
At least one unseen item requiring two simultaneous constraints satisfied by a single factor pair
At least one unseen item where the child selects among candidate products and must justify the selection by its factor structure
All observations tagged unseen, unassisted, independent_probe, with the child's stated reasoning captured verbatim
input.nextAcademicTarget: math.multiplication.synthesis.constrained_factor_pairs_and_impossibility — given a product and two simultaneous structural constraints, generate a valid rectangular arrangement, solve for an unknown factor, or correctly determine that no arrangement exists and justify why.
input.nextMechanic: Drag-to-pack rectangular array building against written shipping orders, with a limited stock of crates, a commit button, and a refusal stamp that is sometimes the only correct answer.
input.nextTheme: Night shift at a harbor packing house. Orders arrive on a conveyor from captains who do not always know what they are asking for.
input.nextOpeningPurpose: The first order on screen is fillable and takes about ten seconds — it teaches the drag, the commit, and the refusal stamp in one motion, and it ends with a captain thanking them, so the child knows the stamp exists and is a real tool before they ever need it.
input.nextCreatorPrompt: Build a boss called "The Impossible Order" for a 9-year-old who has just proved they can re-group a fixed product into different equal groups on unseen material, quickly and happily. Setting: a harbor packing house at night. Orders slide in on a conveyor. Each order names a number of fish (the product) and states TWO rules at once — for example "pack 18 fish, exactly 3 fish per row" or "pack 24 fish, more than 4 rows and more than 4 fish in each row." The child drags fish into a grid to build the array. The grid only accepts complete rows; a half-filled row glows red and will not lock. Below the grid sit two buttons: SHIP IT and CANNOT BE PACKED. Some orders — 17 fish in equal rows of more than one, or 25 fish in exactly 4 equal rows — genuinely have no solution, and the only correct move is the refusal stamp plus choosing a short reason from three options ("nothing divides it evenly," "the rows don't come out even," "the rule breaks the count"). Stock matters: the child begins the shift with a fixed supply of fish. Shipping a wrong order spills that crate into the water — those fish are gone from the shift and the next orders must be filled from less. Refusing a fillable order also costs, because the captain leaves and takes their crate with them. Late in the shift an order arrives that the child cannot fill unless they saved stock earlier. The final order is the hardest kind: a quantity the child chooses from two candidates on the dock, where only one of them can meet the stated rules — they must pick and then build. Escalate from one rule to two rules to a choice of quantity. Keep decisions dense; no long dialogue. End the shift with the harbor master reading back the child's own refusals aloud as the proudest part of the night — refusing an impossible order is what a real packer does. Do not certify mastery in the ending text; the shift ends, the tally is shown, and the record goes to the harbor log.
input.nextStakesDesign: Fish stock is finite and non-renewable within the shift. Every wrong ship spills a crate into the harbor and permanently shrinks the supply the child has for later orders; every wrong refusal loses a paying captain and their crate. Because a late order requires stock the child must still have, early carelessness makes a later order literally unfillable — the child watches an order they understand perfectly slide past because they no longer have the fish. What is at risk is the completeness of the night's manifest, and the child can end the shift with a short, visibly incomplete log that is theirs.
input.nextFailureMode: The shift can be failed. If stock drops below what the remaining orders need, orders start sliding off the conveyor unfilled, and the shift ends early with the harbor log short and gaps marked in it. The two distinct failures are readable and separate: forcing an uneven arrangement through and shipping it (spilled crate) versus stamping CANNOT BE PACKED on an order that was in fact packable (lost captain). Both are recorded by name in the log, so the child sees which mistake was theirs.
input.nextEscalation: Order one is a single rule with an obvious answer, ten seconds, one solution. Orders two through four add a second simultaneous rule so satisfying only one is now a visible failure. Order five is the first genuine impossibility, arriving with no warning among fillable orders so the child must notice it themselves. Orders six through eight mix fillable and impossible unpredictably while stock is already reduced, and the conveyor speed increases slightly so hesitation costs an order. The final order requires the child to choose which of two quantities on the dock can satisfy the rules, refuse the other, and then build the array from remaining stock.
input.nextMechanicSpec: The child drags fish one at a time or in a swipe from a stock bin into a rectangular pen. Fish snap into rows left to right. A row that is not full stays translucent and pulses red; the pen will not lock while any row is incomplete. As fish land, a live readout under the pen updates — "4 rows × 5 fish = 20" — and turns green only when both stated rules are satisfied simultaneously. Pressing SHIP IT with a red readout tips the pen sideways: the fish slide out, splash, and the stock counter drops by that amount with an audible fall — they do not come back. Pressing CANNOT BE PACKED shows a stamp thudding onto the order; if the order was truly impossible, the harbor master nods and the order pins to the log board; if it was packable, the captain's boat pulls away with the crate still aboard and the log board shows an empty slot. On screen, failure looks like an emptying stock bin and a log board with holes in it.
input.nextMathematicalHook: Some numbers are generous and some are stubborn. Twenty-four will rearrange itself into rows of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, or 12 for anyone who asks — but 17 will not break into equal rows at all, no matter how the fish are pushed around, and no amount of trying changes that. The whoa is discovering that "it can't be done" is a real mathematical answer with a reason behind it, and that saying so out loud is a stronger move than forcing a row that doesn't fit.
input.revisedHypothesis: Lab Learner transfers equal-groups, missing-factor, and word-problem interpretation to unseen material at high accuracy, and the uniqueness misconception observed at baseline ("only one pair") has resolved for generation: given a product, Lab Learner now produces alternative valid factor pairs without stalling. What remains untested is the negative case and the multi-constraint case. Prediction: when two constraints must hold at once, Lab Learner will satisfy the more salient rule first and check the second only after building; and when an arrangement is genuinely impossible, Lab Learner will exhaust several near-miss arrangements before considering refusal, and may ship an uneven arrangement rather than assert impossibility — because impossibility has never been modeled as a legitimate answer.
